:topic/_next.:topic/title: Integrating Linear Rational Functions Using Substitution

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We note that $6x^2$ is the derivative of the quantity in the parentheses. So we make a substitution

$$
u=2x^3+3.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=6{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and rewriting our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 6{x}^{2}(2{x}^{3}+3)^{6}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2{x}^{3}+3)^{6}\,6{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{6}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now solve the integral using the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{6}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{{u}^{7}}{7}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we substitute $u=2x^3+3$ back in the expression. So the final result is

$$
\displaystyle\int 6x^2(2x^3+3)^6\,\textrm{d}x =\dfrac{(2x^3+3)^7}{7}+C.
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by Its Derivative

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The $x$ that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $(1+2x^2).$ The derivative of $(1+2x^2)$ is $4x,$ so we're out by a constant factor of $4$. However, since we're out only by a constant factor, substitution will still work!

So we make the substitution

$$
u=1+2x^2.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =4x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{(1+2{x}^{2})}^{6}\,\text{d}x & =\int {(1+2{x}^{2})}^{6}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{6}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{6}\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{6}\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{{u}^{7}}{7}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{28}{u}^{7}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{28}{(1+2{x}^{2})}^{7}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by a Constant Multiple of Its Derivative

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u=x^3+1.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 3x^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 3 \textrm d u= x^2 \, \textrm d x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{3}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}+1}\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{3}+1|+C\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Integrating a Rational Function Using Natural Logarithms

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u = 1 - x^3.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = -3x^2 \quad \Longrightarrow\quad -\dfrac{1}{3} \textrm d u= x^2 \, \textrm d x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{3}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{3}}}\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\cdot (-\frac{1}{3})\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(2\sqrt{u})+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{u}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{1-{x}^{3}}+C\end{aligned}
$$
